read.sections.0.text.source: On 17 August 1945, two leaders, Sukarno and Mohammad Hatta, made a proclamation of independence for Indonesia. The country's National Archives keeps Sukarno's handwritten draft of this short text. For Indonesians, 17 August 1945 is the day of independence. But the Netherlands had ruled the islands as a colony, and it did not accept the proclamation. Years of armed struggle and talks followed. On 27 December 1949, the Netherlands transferred sovereignty. This was a different event from the proclamation. It came after a long struggle. The draft records the 1945 statement. It does not tell us about every talk, or how people lived through those years.
read.sections.0.text.back: On 17 August 1945, two leaders, Sukarno and Mohammad Hatta, made a proclamation of independence for Indonesia. Indonesia's National Archives keeps Sukarno's handwritten draft of this short text. For the people of Indonesia, 17 August 1945 is the day of independence. But the Netherlands had ruled the islands as a colony, and the Netherlands did not accept the proclamation. Years of armed struggle and talks followed. On 27 December 1949, the Netherlands handed over sovereignty. This event was different from the proclamation. This event happened after a long struggle. The draft records the 1945 statement. The draft does not tell us about every talk, or how people lived through those years.

read.sections.0.simpler.source: On 17 August 1945, two leaders made a proclamation. They said Indonesia was free. The two men were Sukarno and Hatta. Sukarno wrote the first draft by hand. The national archives keep it today. The Dutch had ruled the islands as a colony. They did not accept the proclamation. Years of fighting and talks came next. In December 1949, the Dutch passed sovereignty to the new state. That was a new step, not the first one. But for the people there, 1945 is still the year they became free.
read.sections.0.simpler.back: On 17 August 1945, two leaders made a proclamation. They said Indonesia was already free. They were Sukarno and Hatta. Sukarno wrote the first draft by hand. The national archives keep it today. The Dutch had ruled the islands as a colony. The Dutch did not accept the proclamation. Years of fighting and talks followed. In December 1949, the Dutch handed sovereignty to the new state. That was a new step, not the first step. But for the people there, 1945 is still the year they became free.
read.sections.0.simpler.note: Malay uses "Belanda" for both "the Netherlands" and "the Dutch".

read.sections.1.text.source: The Federation of Malaya took a different path. On 8 February 1956, its leaders and Britain signed an agreement in London. It set 31 August 1957 as the day of independence. These are not two rival dates. One is the date of an agreement, and one is the date it planned for. The new country was the Federation of Malaya. Malaysia, a larger federation, was formed later, on 16 September 1963. A path built on talks still had conflict. A long armed conflict called the Malayan Emergency began in 1948. It was declared over only in 1960.
read.sections.1.text.back: The Federation of Malaya followed a different path. On 8 February 1956, its leaders and Britain signed an agreement in London. That agreement set 31 August 1957 as the day of independence. These are not two competing dates. One is the date of the agreement, and the other is the date the agreement planned. The new country was the Federation of Malaya. Malaysia, a bigger federation, was formed later, on 16 September 1963. A path built through talks still had conflict. A long armed conflict, called the Malayan Emergency, began in 1948. The Emergency was declared ended only in 1960.

read.sections.1.simpler.source: Malaya took a different path. In 1956, its leaders and Britain signed an agreement in London. It set a date. On 31 August 1957, the Federation of Malaya became free. A federation is a group of states that work as one. Malaysia came later, in 1963. Malaya's path used talks. But there was also a long armed conflict. It began in 1948. It did not end until 1960.
read.sections.1.simpler.back: Malaya followed a different path. In 1956, its leaders and Britain signed an agreement in London. That agreement set a date. On 31 August 1957, the Federation of Malaya became free. A federation is a group of states that join together as one. Malaysia was formed later, in 1963. Malaya became free through talks. But there was also a long armed conflict. That conflict began in 1948. That conflict only ended in 1960.

read.sections.2.text.source: The two paths had different people, papers, conflicts and choices. A proclamation, an agreement and a ceremony each record a different part of change. The photo shows Stadium Merdeka in Kuala Lumpur in 2025. It shows the place, not the 1957 ceremony. A British news film made on the day shows crowds, guests and the Federation's flag going up. When you compare sources, ask three questions. What happened on this date? Who made the source? What came later? A careful look can show how two paths differ, without calling one of them better.
read.sections.2.text.back: The two paths had different people, documents, conflicts and choices. A proclamation, an agreement and a ceremony each record a different part of change. The photo shows Stadium Merdeka in Kuala Lumpur in 2025. The photo shows the place, not the 1957 ceremony. A British news film made on that day shows the crowds, guests and the Federation's flag being raised. When you compare sources, ask three questions. What happened on this date? Who made this source? What happened later? A careful observation can show how the two paths differ, without saying one path is better.

watch.summary.source: This short film was made in 1957 in Kuala Lumpur by British Pathé, a British company that made news films. It shows the ceremony for the independence of the Federation of Malaya. First, the camera looks down on Stadium Merdeka. The stadium is full of people, and many of them hold umbrellas. Cars arrive, and important guests walk in. The camera moves between the guests and the crowds. People make speeches from a raised stage. Guards stand very still around the field. Near the end, the flag of the Federation is raised. The important guests salute it as it reaches the top of the pole. The film shows one day. It does not show the years of talks that came before it.
watch.summary.back: This short film was made in 1957 in Kuala Lumpur by British Pathé, a British company that made news films. This film shows the independence ceremony of the Federation of Malaya. First, the camera looks down towards Stadium Merdeka. The stadium is full of people, and many of them hold umbrellas. Cars arrive, and important guests walk in. The camera moves between the guests and the crowds. People give speeches from a raised stage. Guards stand upright without moving around the field. Near the end, the Federation's flag is raised. The important guests salute the flag as the flag reaches the top of the pole. This film shows one day. This film does not show the years of talks before it.

sensitiveNotes.0.source: Both paths involved armed conflict: Indonesia's struggle of 1945–1949 and the Malayan Emergency of 1948–1960. The lesson names this plainly and gives no detail; keep it that way, and show no images of fighting. Many popular YouTube videos on Indonesia's revolution show combat and dead bodies, so do not swap one in for the Watch video. Never ask learners about their own or their family's experiences of war, conflict or displacement, or about their home country, religion or ethnicity, and never ask them to compare their own country's history with these. Learners and staff in Indonesia or Malaysia may feel strongly about these dates: present each as that country's own history, not a contest.
sensitiveNotes.0.back: Both paths involved armed conflict: Indonesia's struggle in 1945–1949 and the Malayan Emergency in 1948–1960. This lesson names it clearly without detail; keep it that way, and show no pictures of fighting. Many popular YouTube videos about the Indonesian revolution show fighting and dead bodies, so do not replace the Watch video with one of them. Never ask learners about their own or their family's experiences of war, conflict or displacement, or about their home country, religion or ethnicity, and never ask them to compare their own country's history with this history. Learners and staff in Indonesia or Malaysia may have strong feelings about these dates: present each one as that country's own history, not a contest.

educatorNotes.0.source: Aim: learners compare dated records for the two paths without ranking them. Evidence move: separate 1945 and 1949 for Indonesia, and 1956 and 1957 for the Federation of Malaya, then name 1963 for Malaysia. A sound answer gives a dated comparison and never says that one nation's independence depended only on outside recognition. Misconceptions to address: "Indonesia was only independent in 1949", "Malaya's path had no conflict", and calling 1957 "Malaysia's independence".
educatorNotes.0.back: Aim: learners compare dated records for both paths without ranking them. Evidence step: separate 1945 and 1949 for Indonesia, and 1956 and 1957 for the Federation of Malaya, then name 1963 for Malaysia. A good answer gives a dated comparison and never says that a nation's independence depended only on recognition from outside. Misconceptions to address: "Indonesia was only independent in 1949", "Malaya's path had no conflict", and calling 1957 "Malaysia's independence".

educatorNotes.1.source: Source caveats: Indonesians count independence from 17 August 1945. For decades the Netherlands named 27 December 1949 instead; the Dutch National Archives' teaching page notes that in 2023 the Dutch prime minister said the Netherlands fully accepts that Indonesia became independent on 17 August 1945. The 1949 transfer was to the federal Republic of the United States of Indonesia, replaced by the unitary Republic a year later: keep this in your notes, not as another date for learners. Malaysia was formed in 1963 by the Federation of Malaya, Singapore, Sabah and Sarawak (Brunei did not join). Government and archive pages on both sides use celebratory language; treat it as their perspective. FINAS's long film "Merdeka for Malaya" (1958) is a state-produced source to analyse, not a Watch video, and do not reproduce the National Archives of Malaysia's 1957 photograph without its reuse permission.
educatorNotes.1.back: Source caveats: the people of Indonesia count independence from 17 August 1945. For decades, the Netherlands named 27 December 1949 instead; the Dutch National Archives' teaching page notes that in 2023 the Dutch Prime Minister said the Netherlands fully accepts that Indonesia became independent on 17 August 1945. The 1949 transfer was made to the Republic of the United States of Indonesia, a federation, which was replaced by the unitary Republic a year later: keep this in your notes, not as another date for learners. Malaysia was formed in 1963 by the Federation of Malaya, Singapore, Sabah and Sarawak (Brunei did not join). Government and archive pages on both sides use celebrating language; treat that as their perspective. FINAS's long film "Merdeka for Malaya" (1958) is a government-produced source to analyse, not a Watch video, and do not reproduce the National Archives of Malaysia's 1957 photo without reuse permission.
educatorNotes.1.note: "Republic of the United States of Indonesia" given its usual Malay/Indonesian name, Republik Indonesia Serikat.
